articles.title_orig: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
articles.title_zh: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
articles.content_orig:
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.
Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.
Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured.
The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.
Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils.
Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.
In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.
In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.
“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”
Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.
While many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.
“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”
The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.
The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.

Red light therapy has many benefits: It can help clear acne, reduce wrinkles and even serve as a recovery tool post-workout by reducing muscle fatigue, joint pain and soreness. But what if you wanted to extend some of those benefits to your pet? After all, most pet owners will try anything to help their furry friends live longer and more comfortably.
When it comes to dogs, especially senior dogs , experts say red light therapy can be useful for relieving arthritis pain and inflammation. But how exactly does it work, and is it safe for all dogs? I spoke with veterinarians about the benefits of red light therapy for dogs and how to use a device on your pet. I also rounded up the best products to consider based on my experts’ guidance, as well as options NBC Selected editors tested on their own dogs.
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
Red light therapy is generally safe for dogs, but using it incorrectly can lead to side effects. “The biggest practical risks with higher-powered devices are eye injury and thermal burns,” says Dr. Kate Elden , veterinarian and chief medical officer at Dutch, a pet telehealth company. “Across all the recent trials for arthritis, ear infections and skin issues, we almost never see adverse events reported.”
While red light therapy is usually low-risk when used correctly, that doesn’t mean it’s right for every dog. You should always talk to your veterinarian first, especially if your dog has active tumors (red light can stimulate cell growth and may speed up the growth of cancer cells, says Elden), active bleeding (can prevent clotting, which increases blood loss), reduced skin sensation (may cause nerve damage or injuries if they can’t feel the device getting too warm) or is pregnant (due to lack of safety data), says Dr. Lindsay Kendrick, the medical director at VEG ER for Pets in Boston .
If you got the green light to try red light therapy on your fur baby, consider one of the devices below. (Note: consult with your vet about whether it’s a good fit before you purchase.) Each product below has a minimum four-star average rating from 100 or more customers and/or was directly recommended by NBC Selected staffers.
Capillus, which has provided red light therapy devices for a decade, recently expanded into pet wellness earlier this month. This vest has two rechargeable pads that cover your dog’s back, chest and stomach. It’s also fully adjustable (it has a harness-style design with adjustable buckle straps) and cordless, so you won’t have to worry about your pet getting overly uncomfortable. It has both red light and near-infrared light, which helps reach your pet’s skin and joints and deeper into the tissue. You can change the intensity of the light using a button on each pad, and the vest has a 20-minute timer that automatically turns it off when the time is up. It comes in a medium and large size.
I tried this vest on my 8-year-old, 16-pound Havanese and bichon frise mix Bella, and I was surprised at how easy it was to set up and put on her. Bella hates having anything on her, whether that’s her harness, a sweater or boots. Since the vest is adjustable, it was so easy to find the right fit for Bella (who is mostly fluff), and she actually left it on for the full 20 minutes without much hassle. However, the medium size is slightly big on her, so I wouldn’t recommend it for smaller dogs.
The Celluma Pro is a large panel that can cover your pet’s pain points and provide relief and reduced inflammation, specifically for larger areas (and bigger dogs), according to the brand. The panel is flexible, so you can turn it into whatever shape works for your pet. For example, if your dog has hip pain, you can fold it into an arch-like shape to cover both hips and legs.
“I’ve never used a red light panel like this one before, so I was a bit intimidated by it and didn’t know what to expect,” says NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin , who tested the device with her 1-year-old mutt, Mabel. When she unpacked it, Malin was pleasantly surprised at how clear and straightforward the directions were.
“Because the panel is flexible, I was able to gently bend it to accommodate where my dog was sleeping or sitting. It also comes with a little stand that I attached to prop it up by her bed,” says Malin. Since Mabel only weighs eight pounds, the panel was big enough to cover most of her body. “The panel is a very easy thing to incorporate into my dog’s day, and I love knowing I’m doing something good for her health that doesn’t require much fuss,” she says.
Its rechargeable battery will last between three to 15 cycles, and it weighs less than two pounds, so you can easily take it anywhere. Plus, you can use any of the three modes (aging skin, pain management and acne) on your own skin, too. The brand recommends using it for 30 minutes a day (my experts recommend five to 15 minutes for dogs), but keep in mind it does not have an automatic shut-off feature, so you may want to set a timer.
Unlike the vest, which covers multiple areas at once, Capillus’s Joint Wrap delivers red light and near-infrared light to specific areas on your dog’s body. It comes in one size that’s meant to fit larger breeds, like German shepherds and labrador retrievers, that commonly suffer from joint-related issues, according to the brand. You can wrap it around your pet’s leg and secure it with a Velcro closure to relieve joint pains and inflammation, plus it’s cordless, rechargeable and easily adjustable. It also has a 15-minute auto-off timer, so you don’t have to worry about overdoing it.
If you’re looking for an alternative to red light therapy, or simply hoping for another therapy tool to use in conjunction with a red light device, consider this pet bed from HigherDose, one of our favorite wellness brands. It has PEMF (Pulsed Electromagnetic Field), which uses gentle, low-frequency waves and low-intensity pulses to help improve circulation, reduce inflammation and support cellular health, according to the brand. Research shows that using PEMF sessions daily helps reduce stiffness and discomfort in dogs, and similar to red light therapy, it helps heal post-surgical wounds, fractures and soft-tissue injuries.
HigherDose already has a PEMF mat for humans , and just recently extended its line with a pet bed. I received the bed from the brand to try out, and Bella immediately loved it (which is surprising considering she already has three beds in our house). Plus, it has a machine-washable cover and comfy bolsters for her to rest her head on. It comes in two sizes: small (for cats and small dogs up to 25 pounds) and large (for medium and large dogs up to 75 pounds).

The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote in a post on X on Thursday, referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He allegedly contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times over the course of less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant also allegedly sent disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August 2026 to September 2026 time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
In one message, Proia allegedly wrote to Miller’s mother, calling Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message allegedly featured a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia allegedly wrote, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, the agency’s Washington Field Office’s assistant director in charge, said in a statement to Bloomberg that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Discovery of Exquisite Feathered Dinosaur in China Could Rewrite The Evolution of Flight
articles.title_zh: Discovery of Exquisite Feathered Dinosaur in China Could Rewrite The Evolution of Flight
articles.content_orig:
An exquisitely preserved feathered raptor just discovered in north-eastern China could probably fly.
It's also somewhat disrupted the evolutionary path we thought birds took to get into the air.
Norellraptor barsboldi, as the new dinosaur has been named, is a microraptor, which means it's a small dinosaur with feathers and wings.
It's also a member of the wider group Paraves , which includes a range of theropod dinosaurs , including some that are still thriving today: birds.
And, like its living relatives, Norellraptor could probably fly.
But close analysis of this remarkably detailed fossil suggests the evolutionary path to flight may be far more forked than we thought.
Norellraptor is described in a new paper by paleontologist Xuri Wang of the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and his colleagues. The paper is published in Nature Communications .
The microraptor's body is 57 centimeters long (just over 22 inches), and based on its bones, the researchers think it hadn't quite finished growing at the time of its death.
Its feathers are much less well-preserved than its bones, but from what the researchers could see, its forelimbs and tail seem to have been festooned with flight-related plumage, while other parts of its body were covered in straight, simple feathers.
Certain features in this Norellraptor's bones, and a close look at where it sits in the Paraves family tree has led the researchers to question what we know about how flight evolved within Paraves.
The fact that both microraptors and birds evolved the ability to fly doesn't necessarily mean they inherited the trait from the same ancestor.
Norellraptor 's current position in the Paraves family tree suggests flight may have actually arisen at least twice, independently.
The steps it followed to reach the skies seem to be quite different from those taken by birds.
Another bit of evidence is that the development of the dinosaur's forearm, or wing, seems to have stopped quite early in its life, which is the opposite of what we see in modern, flying birds.
"The sequences of flight-related novelties reconstructed along the two lineages differ consistently," Wang and team write .
"Combined with histological evidence which might indicate a peculiar limb growth model in Microraptorinae, these results dismiss a shared developmental pattern driving the evolution of the flying dinosaurs and support multiple and independent selective regimes at the origin of the winged taxa in Paraves."
In other words, there might have been some convergent evolution going on in the Paraves family.
That's when two separate evolutionary groups reach a similar outcome via a totally different route. Think whales and fishes: both can swim using fins, but they arrived at that body plan from totally different paths.
Still, paleontologists can't rely on just one fossil to rewrite evolutionary history.
A lot more evidence will be needed before scientists are convinced that birds and microraptors did indeed evolve flight entirely independently.
"Microraptorines have been advocated as models for investigating the origin and evolution of the avian flight," the authors note .
"Yet, the evolutionary relationships between the flight apparatus of birds and the purported aerial adaptations of the microraptorines are controversial from both functional and phylogenetic perspectives."
The research has been published in Nature Communications .

articles.title_orig: Reflecting Pool vandalism charges against Olympic canoeist David Hearn permanently dismissed
articles.title_zh: Reflecting Pool vandalism charges against Olympic canoeist David Hearn permanently dismissed
articles.content_orig:
Former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, left, and his attorney Norm Eisen, right, leave D.C. court with a smile in early September after a hearing about the dismissal of his vandalism charges. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
A judge has dismissed with prejudice the government's vandalism charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. That means federal prosecutors cannot refile them in the future, despite President Trump's public demands to do so.
In fact, as D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman explained in a 26-page ruling released Thursday, the case should be permanently closed in large part because of the "political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers."
"While the prosecutors admit that the evidence indicates that he committed no crime, the President's statements create a risk that Mr. Hearn will be prosecuted nonetheless, either because the current United States Attorney and her assistants will eventually yield to his public pressure campaign or because the President will replace them with prosecutors more likely to carry out his wishes," wrote Edelman, an Obama appointee.
Hearn, 67, was arrested at the Reflecting Pool in June, around the time its multimillion-dollar new blue lining started noticeably peeling off in chunks. He was charged with one felony count of property destruction and quickly indicted by a grand jury , though he pleaded not guilty .
In late July, however, with a trial start date — and the prospect of up to 10 years in prison if convicted — looming, Pirro's office abruptly asked the judge to drop the charges against Hearn and three others altogether.
Citing new reports from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, federal prosecutors admitted that the Reflecting Pool damage was, in fact, "the result of botched installation and not vandalism."
Trump disagreed, and publicly urged Pirro to revisit the case — which Thursday's ruling prevents.
When asked for comment, the White House referred NPR to three of Trump's Truth Social posts from August, blaming the Reflecting Pool damage on vandals and disagreeing with U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro's decision to drop charges against Hearn in the first place.
Hearn's supporters rally outside the District of Columbia Courthouse during an early September hearing. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
Neither the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. nor the Department of Justice returned NPR's requests for comment in time for publication.
Hearn's lawyers — Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — celebrated the ruling in a joint statement, calling it "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," they said. "This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American."
The soft-spoken Maryland resident quickly became a cause célèbre for the many Americans captivated by the Reflecting Pool saga , which some saw as a referendum on the Trump administration itself.
In an August interview with NPR , Hearn described his experience as "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian," but said he was buoyed by the support he'd received from within and beyond his community.
"With the power of the law, the power of the courts, and my wonderful team, I feel very well equipped … to bring democracy back to me," he said.
Trump railed against Pirro in the days and weeks after she dropped the charges, saying she had "choked" and "folded like an umbrella" — and didn't rule out firing her. He continued to blame the damage on vandalism and wrote on social media that anyone who disagreed "should go back to Law School."
"Most concerningly," Edelman wrote, during that time, the president also leveled increasingly personal attacks against Hearn and his legal team.
"U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue, a disgraceful fundraising SCAM, and is represented by a TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG, Political Hack Lawyer, Norm Eisen," Trump wrote in early August , in one of the social media posts the White House directed NPR to on Thursday.
It's against that backdrop that Hearn's legal team has been lobbying the judge to dismiss the charges with prejudice, to prevent the same case from being revived. The Trump administration, on the other hand, sought to leave that door open.
Edelman's Thursday ruling offers a peek into the government's argument — and then dismantles it.
The empty, fenced-off Reflecting Pool as seen in late September. Rod Lamkey/AP hide caption
Edelman wrote that when asked in court what kind of hypothetical new evidence might prompt prosecutors to revisit the case, an unnamed assistant U.S. attorney "waxed philosophical, musing, 'I don't know what the future may bring. None of us do.'"
He says prosecutors could not provide any specific examples of such evidence, and "admitted that the government was no longer even investigating the case."
"Given its own description of the existing evidence and the circumstances of this case, the development of contrary evidence seems practically inconceivable, and the possibility of a future meritorious prosecution strikes the Court as fanciful," Edelman concluded.
Hearn's lawyers say Thursday's ruling allows him "to move forward with his life as he deserves."
The Reflecting Pool, which was drained after July 4th, remains empty and fenced off for repairs, with no public timeline for completion.

articles.title_zh: Lindsay Clancy lawyer’s bid to get killer mom’s murder charges tossed is slapped down
articles.content_orig:
By RACHEL SHARP, CRIME CORRESPONDENT and JOE HUTCHISON, US SENIOR NEWS REPORTER
Published: 15:49 EDT, 1 October 2026 | Updated: 18:59 EDT, 1 October 2026
Lindsay Clancy has lost her legal bid to be found not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility for murdering her three children.
The 36-year-old former nurse had asked Judge William Sullivan to acquit her on all charges because the state failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt and present sufficient evidence of her guilt.
In what marked her first court hearing since a mistrial was declared earlier this months, Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington argued on Tuesday that the prosecution's evidence was insufficient in two areas: both proving the identity of the 'individual who committed the crimes' and her 'criminal responsibility.'
On Thursday, Judge Sullivan denied the motion writing that the evidence on both areas 'was sufficient to have satisfied any rational trier of fact beyond a reasonable doubt.'
Clancy is facing the prospect of being tried a second time after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict at the end of her six-week trial.
The mom-of-three was charged with three counts of first-degree murder for killing Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months old, inside the family home in the wealthy suburb of Duxbury, Massachusetts, on January 24, 2023 .
The 36-year-old labor and delivery nurse strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement after sending her husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the home to run errands.
She then tried to kill herself, cutting her wrists and neck and jumping from the second-floor bedroom window. Clancy survived but was left paralyzed from the waist down.
Clancy speaks with her lawyer Kevin Reddington during proceedings in her murder trial
Justice William F. Sullivan denied the motion writing that the evidence 'was sufficient to have satisfied any rational trier of fact beyond a reasonable doubt'
She did not deny killing her children but pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, saying she was suffering from severe postpartum depression and psychosis at the time.
After 38 hours of deliberations, the 12 jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict and, on September 4, a mistrial was declared. It turned out that a lone holdout juror, identified as Michael Desronvil, refused to join the other 11 in finding her not guilty by reason of insanity.
Inside Plymouth County Superior Court, Massachusetts , on Tuesday, Reddington argued that the judge should return a finding of not guilty because there was no evidence that she even killed her children.
'This entire case is based on speculation. Where is the admission? Where did she say that she did this?' he asked.
Gesturing animatedly inside the jam-packed courtroom, he claimed that the former nurse had been demonized by everyone, including the president.
‘She's a demon and possessed and should be executed,' he claimed people were saying. 'This is coming from politicians, from President Trump, all the way down.'
Slamming the entire investigation into the children’s deaths, Reddington questioned: 'Where is the evidence that she did this?'
Sitting wheelchair-bound at the defense table, Clancy watched as Reddington and the prosecution sparred over whether she should stand trial for a second time.
Reddington argued there was no blood on Clancy's socks after she cut herself and leaped from the bedroom window and, when she woke from a coma, she had no memory of killing her children, he said.
Clancy was charged with murder after strangling her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan in 2023
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington questioned the investigation into Clancy as he argued for a required finding of not guilty
Instead, she was simply told by police that she had killed her children despite there being issues with the timeline of that day, he argued.
Because of the shoddy investigation, the state had no probable cause that she was even the perpetrator of the crime, he claimed.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham branded his comments ‘laughable,’ saying this was the first time the defense had made this claim.
As well as lacking probable cause, Reddington also argued that there is no sufficient evidence to prove the 36-year-old is criminally responsible for the killings.
For a defendant to be found criminally responsible, a jury must determine two things: whether or not she was suffering a mental defect or disease at the time, and whether or not she could still control her actions or conform to the law despite her mental illness.
Reddington argued that the prosecution failed to prove its case on both points.
Firing back, Buckingham argued that a defendant who suffers from mental illness can commit crimes and still be criminally responsible.
Judge Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement and rule at a later date - before handing down his ruling on Thursday.
Several other motions and arguments are yet to be decided by the judge.
Arguments about the defense’s request to investigate the lone holdout juror, a defense motion to dismiss the case on double jeopardy grounds, and a motion from the state requesting a gag order preventing Reddington from speaking out about the case were all put on pause.
A date of November 2 was set for a follow-up hearing where those matters will be argued.
No new trial date was set – after the two sides both asked the judge to delay the matter and Reddington said he would not be available for a retrial until June.
Judge Sullivan told the lawyers to prepare to set a date at the November 2 hearing.
As it stands, the prosecution is yet to confirm whether or not it will retry Clancy and, if so, on the same charges of first-degree murder or lesser charges.
When asked by reporters outside court, Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz said his office was still deciding its next course of action.

articles.title_zh: Joey Porter Jr. felt "disrespected" and "underappreciated" by Steelers
articles.content_orig:
The Dallas Cowboys traded with the Pittsburgh Steelers for cornerback Joey Porter Jr. on Thursday.
The question that arose after the trade, though, is whether or not Porter would be healthy to play for the Cowboys in Week 4 versus the Houston Texans. Porter has yet to make his 2026 season debut as he's been sidelined with a back injury. He missed training camp and the first three games of the season with the Steelers.
However, Porter was also in the midst of a contract dispute with Pittsburgh after a disagreement about guaranteed money. ESPN's Ed Werder reported on Thursday that Porter was OK with playing in Dallas without a contract extension "because the Cowboys are the team he most wanted to play for."
When speaking with Dallas media for the first time on Thursday, Porter said his back is "feeling better," but he didn't commit to playing on Sunday.
“We’re just trying to take things day by day, and if everything looks good, then we should be out there," Porter said, via ESPN's Todd Archer .
Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer also sounded hopeful for Porter to start on Sunday, but he didn't give him an official designation.
"We'd like him to play, but we'll see how the week goes. I think he's excited about the opportunity to maybe play, but we'll see how the rest of the week goes," Schottenheimer said. "But it was a good start today."
It's definitely interesting timing that Porter quickly feels ready to play after landing with a new team. Especially since on Wednesday, one day before the trade, the Steelers ruled Porter out for their "Thursday Night Football" contest versus the Cleveland Browns. Pittsburgh coach Mike McCarthy was originally hopeful Porter would start in Week 4 after participating in a limited capacity at practice this week. But, his lingering back issue caused a problem on Wednesday to rule him out.
Granted, Porter now has three extra days to prepare to play since the Cowboys don't play until Sunday. But, it would be a quick and suspicious turnaround if the cornerback is ready to play this week.

Halle Berry’s ex-husband Olivier Martinez has been granted primary custody of their son, Maceo, after he accused the actress of choking their 12-year-old .
The restraining order was granted Thursday, with the “Monster’s Ball” actress losing 50/50 custody in lieu of daytime visits with Maceo, Page Six has confirmed.
Berry will be able to see her son during court-ordered visitation, which is two days a week and every other weekend.
In addition, Berry is ordered to not come within 100 yards of Martinez.
The next court date for the exes is set for Oct. 16.
Berry denied Martinez’s shocking allegations through her attorney, who called the filing “entirely meritless and deliberately misleading.”
“There is voluminous evidence, including numerous judicial rulings, that Olivier Martinez repeatedly violated court orders and interfered with necessary therapeutic and educational interventions to the detriment of his and Halle Berry’s minor son Maceo — misconduct for which Mr. Martinez has already been legally sanctioned,” the actress’ attorney, Marina Beck, shared in a statement with Page Six Thursday.
She also claimed Martinez has a well-documented history of “erratic, possessive and violent behavior.”
“Halle is used to this kind of outrageous conduct from Mr. Martinez and, while she is deeply saddened, she will not allow it to deter her from fighting for Maceo’s best interests and providing him with the love and support he needs,” the statement concluded.
On Sept. 26, Berry allegedly jumped on Maceo, put her hands around his neck and choked him, Martinez claimed in court docs obtained by Page Six.
The French actor claimed the argument began after Berry told Maceo he looked “stupid” and was “such an idiot” for playing a game with his virtual reality goggles.
“The situation escalated and Petitioner jumped on our son and started physically fighting with him,” Martinez alleged in the docs. “She grabbed Maceo by the neck and started choking him while shouting, ‘Who is dominant now?! Who is dominant?!’ ”
Martinez claimed that a panicked Maceo called him to pick him up after the alleged incident — and said he doesn’t want to return to his mom’s house due to being “traumatized.”

Boeing engineers and technical workers approved a sweetened four-year contract with immediate 10% raises, avoiding a potential strike at the aerospace giant as it seeks federal approval for new aircraft and to increase aircraft production.
"We secured many victories that some thought were completely out of reach when this negotiation cycle started," said the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace, which represents about 13,000 Boeing engineers and 4,000 technical workers.
Boeing increased its offer in mid-September after the workers rejected an earlier proposal. In addition to the 10% ratification wage increase, the four-year contract includes annual raises of 4%, with an increase of up to 6% based on merit.
The professional unit, which includes engineers, voted 67.62% in favor of the new contract, and the tech unit approved the contract with 53.48% in favor, the union said.
The work groups, which make up Boeing's largest white-collar union, overwhelmingly rejected an earlier offer with 3% annual raises.
Boeing said in a statement that it was "pleased with the outcome of the vote."
The approval lets Boeing avoid a strike just as it's trying to stabilize and increase production of its fast-selling jets and win federal approval for the 737 Max 10 and 777X, which are years behind schedule.
The Federal Aviation Administration on Monday said it's assessing whether a software issue on the 737 Max 10, which could affect landing procedures in certain scenarios, poses a safety of flight issue.
A machinist strike two years ago halted production until the two sides reached a deal.

articles.title_zh: 'They’ll be hit very hard': Trump sends 9,000 troops to the Middle East after warning Iran strikes
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. military is dispatching roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned anew that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The troop movement, which includes a third aircraft carrier, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump’s war against Iran as he ponders his next move, with midterm elections in the United States looming large and new signs that the nature of the conflict may be becoming more complex.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation — despite his initial promises to Americans of a campaign that would last a matter of weeks — remains a viable option. Further complicating matters, Trump told reporters Thursday that early indications suggest that Iran is linked to the FlyDubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain and tried to crash an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday.
In an exchange with reporters at the White House, Trump raised the connection when asked by a reporter if there were any links between the pilot behind the attack and Tehran.
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is ‘yes,’ but we’re working on it right now,” Trump said, without offering details.
Trump added that if the link to Iran is established, the United States would retaliate. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a Fox News interview earlier Thursday that investigators believe the FlyDubai suspect underwent “Islamist, radical indoctrination” but did not provide further details.
“Oh, they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry,” Trump said. “You just ask them. They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
Meanwhile, the group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines.
It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, which recently deployed with the cruiser USS Chosin, and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the U.S. official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the U.S. naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group. The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
Trump, in a Time magazine interview published Thursday, also raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is “possible” that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the Nov. 3 elections in the United States.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
“I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?” Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up” the Strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough.”
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican Party chances in November, Trump at first responded, “It’s possible.” But then he added, “It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
The president said “100% of the people” oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities “including worldwide.”
“So, when you say it that way, it would help,” Trump added. “If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”
Yet, there’s also growing concern that Tehran might be turning to asymmetrical tactics following the FlyDubai attack and another suspicious incident in the U.K.
Authorities believe that Iran might be looking to shift strategy just as the U.S. finds greater success in loosening Iran’s grip over the Strait of Hormuz and getting Gulf allies’ oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran’s own oil exports.
British authorities announced on Thursday the arrest of a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran .
The arrest of the 27-year-old man in Central London came after U.K. authorities arrested five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, in the early hours of Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base
The base has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail .

Bolivian police arrested the country’s top prosecutor and 13 others accused of protecting drug traffickers, the government said Thursday, days after the Trump administration imposed visa restrictions on the attorney general and several senior officials over corruption allegations.
The arrest of Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca, appointed to a six-year term in 2024 under Bolivia’s previous socialist government, comes as conservative President Rodrigo Paz deepens security cooperation with Washington . U.S. Secretary State Marco Rubio hailed the arrests as “bold and decisive actions to combat narco-trafficking, systemic corruption, and transnational organized crime in Bolivia.”
Mariaca did not immediately comment on his arrest but had earlier denounced U.S. accusations that he accepted bribes to facilitate drug trafficking as political pressure on his office. Anti-drug prosecutor Miguel Gonzales said late Wednesday that police had detained Mariaca without a warrant.
“We have dismantled a criminal organization entrenched in the justice system,” Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo told reporters Thursday, adding that Mariaca would face charges of money laundering and drug trafficking.
Authorities detained but swiftly released suspected Uruguayan drug kingpin Sebastián Marset in 2023, when Mariaca was chief prosecutor in the eastern region of Santa Cruz, Oviedo said. “They let him go, and not only that, they returned his seized assets,” he said of the longtime fugitive trafficker. Marset was ultimately captured in Bolivia last March and sent to the U.S. to face money laundering charges.
Oviedo also alleged that bundles of cash seized from an ambulance leaving Mariaca’s home in the city of Santa Cruz early Thursday were proceeds of extortion targeting people who sought help from prosecutors. Prosecutor Daniel Ortuño said officers found 3.53 million bolivianos (about $294,000) and an additional $10,000 in the vehicle.
The other detainees included two prosecutors also targeted by this week’s U.S. visa sanctions, part of a broader round of travel bans affecting over a dozen officials across South America.
The State Department cast Monday's measures as support for the Shield of the Americas, the Trump administration's security alliance with mostly conservative governments in the region, including Bolivia, to fight organized crime. The restrictions marked the latest instance of Washington using U.S. visas to pressure critics and officials whose actions conflict with its priorities in Latin America.
Urging lawmakers to overhaul the justice system, Oviedo warned officials against cooperating with criminal groups.
“Either you stand with the law ... or you stand with crime, with narcoterrorism,” he said.
Paz took office last November, ending nearly two decades of dominance by the Movement Toward Socialism party of former President Evo Morales . He has warmed ties with Washington and resumed cooperation with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, which Morales expelled along with the U.S. ambassador in 2008, accusing them of seeking to overthrow his government.

China’s major refiners have suspended most refined fuel exports for October as Beijing prioritizes domestic supply security, removing another source of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel from an already severely constrained global market.
PetroChina has cancelled several gasoline and jet fuel cargoes scheduled for October, while Zhejiang Petrochemical did not schedule exports during China’s week-long National Day holiday, Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the matter. Beijing has yet to authorize October exports outside Hong Kong and Macau, although shipments could resume after the holiday ends on October 7 depending on domestic inventories and refinery output.
The move follows a sharp deterioration in China’s own fuel-stock position. Kpler estimates commercial diesel and gasoil inventories are around 20 million barrels below pre-war levels, while gasoline stocks are roughly 9 million barrels short of the threshold Beijing wants restored before allowing exports to normalize.
China had significantly increased exports during the summer. Official customs data showed total oil-product exports reached 6.01 million tonnes in August, up 12.7% year-on-year and the highest since March 2024, according to S&P Global. At the time, Chinese refiners said Beijing had not yet restricted clean-product exports despite tightening domestic supply.
The reversal comes as global diesel supplies are already being squeezed by Middle Eastern disruptions and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. S&P Global warned this week that Asian fuel markets have limited surplus supply, meaning any further restriction on U.S. diesel exports would increase competition for Asian and Middle Eastern barrels.
China’s own government has meanwhile intervened to limit the domestic impact of high international oil prices, partially suppressing scheduled gasoline and diesel price increases in September while instructing refiners to ensure stable supplies.

articles.title_orig: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal Minneapolis shooting
articles.title_zh: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal Minneapolis shooting
articles.content_orig:
The family of an American woman shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has filed two civil lawsuits related to her death, according to court records filed Thursday in Minnesota federal court.
Renee Good was killed January 7 by ICE agent Jonathan Ross in Minneapolis during the height of the Department of Homeland Security’s Operation Metro Surge, prompting significant protest in the city and sparking national outrage.
“The hole in my family and myself, created by my sister’s passing, is hauntingly apparent,” Good’s brother and plaintiff, Brent Ganger, said at a Thursday news conference announcing the lawsuits.
“Since Renee’s death, no meaningful change has occurred. The deaths of innocent Americans by taxpayer-funded government agents should not be a partisan issue, and it should alarm every American.”
One lawsuit names the United States of America as the sole defendant under the Federal Tort Claims Act , a federal law that allows people to sue the US government for personal injury, property damage or death, caused by alleged negligence of federal employees acting within their job duties.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory damages for Good’s partner, who witnessed the shooting, and “for the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” the family’s attorneys said in a statement.
We're tracking shootings, arrests and deportations in Trump's immigration crackdown. Here's the latest
In January, attorneys sent letters to the federal agencies connected with Good’s death, notifying them of their intention to pursue legal action. Under FTCA guidelines, they waited six months for a response, which could be a denial, agreement to payment, or simply a non-response, attorney Sarah Raisch said.
“We are here today because we have not heard from the government, either that they will accept the claim, or not,” attorney Antonio Romanucci said.
A tort lawsuit against the federal government, from guilt or innocence to the amount of a potential award, is typically decided by a federal judge.
In their second lawsuit, Good’s family alleges, among other things, Operation Metro Surge was “a carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors” to interfere with the civil rights of Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin, and to silence “the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign.”
The suit names Ross, ten John Doe federal agents, and several current and former Trump administration officials as defendants, including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, White House border czar Tom Homan, former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem, and Greg Bovino , the former Border Patrol official who led the administration’s immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis.
Lawyers for Renee Good’s family have experience taking on the government, but this time they face more hurdles
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the Trump administration intends “to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits.”
Bis also pointed to President Donald Trump’s remarks to CBS News about Good from January, in which he said “I love all of our people … and I would bet you that she, under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person. But, you know, her actions were pretty tough.” Trump also defended ICE, saying the job of federal agents was “being made very difficult.”
CNN has reached out to DHS, and phone numbers listed under Noem’s name for comment. Bovino declined to comment about the lawsuit.
The lawsuit alleges the shots fired by Ross were “the predictable and intended product of the operation,” according to the family’s attorneys.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages.
Good’s partner and plaintiff, Becca Good, spoke publicly for the first time since the deadly shooting took place. During the Thursday news conference, she called Good “the center” of her universe and spoke about taking their 6-year-old son to first grade without her.
“Living without her is like trying to live without the sun. And you don’t know how much light something gives you until it’s gone, and then you feel that absence every single second,” she said, becoming emotional.
Renee Good loved her three children, her partner said, and enjoyed reading them books, and talking about music and comics with them.
“Every morning, she is my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama, and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” she said. “But I also think a lot about what she would have wanted after all of this.”
Becca Good said the family is pursuing legal action because “Renee’s love and legacy demand a better world for her children, for this community, and for this country.”
“What happened to us should never happen to any family,” Good said. “Accountability and change — true accountability — is the only way to make sure that no other family has to go through what we have.”
“I don’t hate the people who took Renee from us, but what I want them to understand is - every single day, they get to look at their children, and their wives, and their sisters, and know what they took from our family,” Good said. “They took a mother away from her children. They know that, and they will carry it forever.”
Good, a mother of three , had just finished dropping her 6-year-old son off at school when she encountered ICE agents.
The moments leading up to the shooting were captured by bystanders as well as Ross , a 10-year ICE veteran, whose cellphone video starts with him in front of Good’s burgundy SUV . The vehicle was stopped for a few minutes perpendicular to a snowy residential Minneapolis street, obstructing the flow of traffic.
Ross did not say anything as he walked from the front of the car toward the driver’s side.
Good then addressed Ross, the video shows.
“That’s fine, dude. I’m not mad at you,” she says. Ross didn’t respond.
Becca Good was standing outside the car and said “show your face” to Ross, whose masked reflection is seen on the vehicle’s windows as he continues walking around it. Becca Good holds her cellphone up, seemingly recording Ross, and tells him, “You wanna come at us? You wanna come at us? I say go get yourself some lunch, big boy.”
She then tries to get back into the car, but the door is locked.
Another officer then tells Renee Good to “get out of the f**king car.”
Renee Good is then seen reversing the car and glancing forward as she turns the steering wheel to the right. The car moves forward, Ross cries out, “whoa,” and three gunshots are heard. Good was shot shortly after 9:30 a.m., according to a news release from the city government.
The video filmed by Ross captured audio of gunshots but doesn’t show the actual moment of the shooting, though other video from bystanders shows Ross was standing out of the vehicle’s path when he opened fire. He fired first into her windshield and then at close range through the open driver’s side window, videos show .
The end of Ross’s video shows the SUV as it barrels forward. Someone can be heard saying, “f**king b*tch.”
DHS later said Good “weaponized her vehicle” to run over an officer near an ICE vehicle.
The search for accountability for the shooting remains ongoing. In March , the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office and two state agencies sued the Trump administration for access to evidence in Good’s shooting death as well as the death of Alex Pretti, who was killed by DHS agents in January.
In July, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the Department of Justice had provided a trove of materials related to both shootings to state investigators. No charges have been filed in either case.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Supreme Court grievance grows as new term looms
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Supreme Court grievance grows as new term looms
articles.content_orig:
Asked specifically what he wants from his Supreme Court nominees, the president replied, “I do like loyalty, yeah.”
Donald Trump’s tantrum in February after the Supreme Court rejected his tariffs policy was extreme , even by his standards. The president not only condemned the six-member majority as “a disgrace to our nation,” but he also insisted that the justices who dared to rule in a way he didn’t like were “very unpatriotic and disloyal to our Constitution.”
Asked then whether he regretted nominating Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch, Trump didn’t answer the question directly, though he said he considers their role in the ruling “an embarrassment to their families.”
In his latest Time magazine interview, the president was even more direct on the subject. From the article :
Yet with so much at stake — for the country and the world, for his party and his own power — Trump can seem curiously preoccupied. During a 75-minute Oval Office interview with TIME, he was discursive and grievance-fueled, veering from the crises of his presidency to resentments old and emerging. He said he regretted appointing Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court, after they ruled against him on tariffs, mail ballots, and birthright citizenship. “I gave them the position of a lifetime,” he said, “and they voted against me often.”
The transcript of the interview added remarkable details. Asked specifically if he regretted nominating Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett, Trump said he did — and then he kept going.
“The Democrats stick like glue — those three, they virtually never vary,” the president said, referring to Justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson. “You can come up with the worst thing in the world and they’ll vote as a group. And while I don’t like it, there’s something I admire about it: There’s loyalty. So they have loyalty to Barack Hussein Obama. They have loyalty to Biden, even though Biden doesn’t even know who the hell they are. He wouldn’t know. He doesn’t even know what the Supreme Court is.”
The petty and unhinged whining didn’t stop there. After an additional harangue about the birthright citizenship and tariff rulings — which really weren’t close calls, and which legal experts of every ideological stripe expected him to lose — Time asked, “You mentioned the word loyalty a moment ago. Is that what you want from your Supreme Court picks?”
The president replied, “I do like loyalty, yeah.”
To be sure, the rhetoric was not altogether surprising. As recently as April, Trump declared by way of his social media platform that “certain” conservative justices on the court have “gone weak, stupid, and bad.” A month later, on Mother’s Day, Trump broke new ground, publishing a 544-word screed in which he said Gorsuch and Barrett “have hurt our Country so badly!” He added, “[I]t’s really OK for them to be loyal to the person that appointed them.”
The problem with these rants isn’t just the impropriety or errors of fact and judgment. Collectively, what they also offer is a reminder that Trump still doesn’t understand how the government works in the United States.
As he sees it, if his administration does something illegal, then it’s incumbent on Supreme Court justices he appointed to simply look the other way — out of “loyalty.”
Indeed, Trump seems utterly baffled by the idea that he could appoint Supreme Court justices who, in turn, sometimes evaluates cases on the merits, which is, the last time I checked, their literal job. In other words, the president keeps publicly complaining not about justices being corrupt, but about justices not being corrupt enough to make him happy.
It’s tempting to think Trump would keep these attitudes private, perhaps limiting his complaints to close allies behind closed doors, but he instead keeps sharing them publicly, as if it were normal for a president to make these ridiculous complaints.

articles.title_orig: Chris Hansen Confronts ‘Primetime’: The Tragic Ending, Seeing His Love Life Onscreen and Considering Legal Action Against A24 Because ‘They Exploited Me’
articles.title_zh: Chris Hansen Confronts ‘Primetime’: The Tragic Ending, Seeing His Love Life Onscreen and Considering Legal Action Against A24 Because ‘They Exploited Me’
articles.content_orig:
“ Primetime ” is a box office overachiever , but the subject of the A24 film calls it a “complete work of fiction.”
Lance Oppenheim’s movie centers on “To Catch a Predator,” the popular “Dateline” segment that ran from 2004 to 2007. In the show, an advocacy group with adult decoys posing as children would chat with online predators in order to lure them to a house, ostensibly to have sex with a minor. But instead of their prey, they would be met by host Chris Hansen (played by Robert Pattinson), who would interrogate the predators about why they were pursuing illicit and illegal affairs. The suspects were then arrested by law enforcement waiting outside the house.
The film is based more specifically on the 2009 Esquire article “Tonight on ‘Dateline’ This Man Will Die,” which chronicled an episode of the show involving Louis William Conradt Jr., an assistant district attorney in Murphy, Texas, who died by suicide after being caught in a police sting conducted in coordination with the “Predator” team.
Hansen is continuing his work on his media platform, TruBlu , which hosts shows such as the spiritual successor to “Predator,” “Takedown With Chris Hansen,” which launched in 2022.
Variety spoke with Hansen a few days after he watched “Primetime.” He discussed his perspective on its box office success, which parts are most upsetting to his former colleagues and what legal action he might take against A24.
No. The only elements of the movie that are not fictionalized are the fact that he uses my name and two or three catchphrases. Everything else is fictionalized. Yes, there was an assistant DA who tragically took his own life, but the circumstances surrounding it, the timeline, the events, it may be based on reality, but none of it is truthful. It’s a complete work of fiction.
Look, nobody wants to see somebody take their own life. But in this case, you had a public official, an assistant district attorney who prosecuted criminal cases, who, according to the police and evidence gathered in the case, conducted sexually explicit conversations with decoys posing as two different teenage boys. In Texas, like many other states, that constitutes a felony. Now, he didn’t show up at the house, but the police made a decision to get a warrant based on probable cause. And I think if you were to talk to the police making those decisions, they would tell you that there was some concern that evidence might be destroyed and that they were going to go serve that arrest warrant at his home.
Now, obviously, we knew they were gonna do this, and we captured the action from the street. And when they went in, according to Murphy police, he had a gun in his hand. He said, “I’m not going to hurt you guys,” and took his own life. Later, Texas Rangers did an investigation, and they determined that on that computer from which he was trying to extract the hard drive, there was child sexually abusive material. As a prosecutor, he knew that in Texas, you could potentially face 10 years in prison for each of those images. So nobody can tell you exactly why Bill Conradt took his own life. Nobody wanted to see it happen. It’s tragic for his family. It’s tragic for him. But to insinuate that there was some push on our part to go arrest him or get him or to find him or to cajole him, it just didn’t happen. He surfaced like any other alleged predator did in an investigation. The decoys don’t go try to find them. They conduct the investigation, and they find us.
The rules on it are very, very explicit. But we have caught a number of high-profile people. We were in San Francisco on a sting last month, and an Ivy League-educated lawyer who ran a multimillion-dollar investment fund showed up in the middle of the day to sexually exploit a 6- and 13-year-old boy whose father he thought was going to take part in the sex act. We don’t look for people; they find us. The whole premise of the movie is false. It’s a fake narrative. It didn’t happen. If that was the case and the police wanted to make a big splash publicitywise, wouldn’t you think they’d wait till Monday when he was sitting in his office at the district attorney’s office and barge in and get him and walk him out of there? That’s what they would have done. Everybody wants to say that this was done for clicks and ratings, and it wasn’t; it was just part of an investigation.
If anybody would take a moment, as some content creators have, and actually look at the story that we did on that particular case, and look at what we did on “The Today Show” the next morning, we were painstakingly transparent about what happened, how it happened and, as much as we knew, why it happened, as we have been with this franchise from the very beginning, continuing through today when we do these investigations which we now call “Takedown With Chris Hansen.” Any sense that anybody involved was pushing forward or that there was a ratings-hungry producer, none of that is true. Even the notion of the name of the film, “Primetime” — “Dateline” has always been on primetime television. It wasn’t like it was at 2 o’clock in the morning, and we were trying to get it on primetime. It was always on primetime. No discussion in that film ever happened.
There are people who think that we have historically worked too closely with law enforcement. But my argument is that’s the only way to be socially responsible and to ensure that there’s justice served in these cases. In the first two investigations, we didn’t collaborate with law enforcement. We didn’t know what was going to happen, but it became very clear in the third investigation that we needed to have a law enforcement presence. That has evolved over the past 22 years into what I think is the best possible way of doing this. That is to ensure justice and to ensure the chain of custody of evidence is secure. And also, look, it doesn’t matter how horrifying the crime is, everybody in this country is entitled to a vigorous defense. So the materials that we capture, obviously, everybody has access to that. Whether you’re the prosecutor or the defense, everybody deserves their fair day in court.
It’s par for the course. You know, even the filmmakers will tell you that this is fiction. And, you know, even when something reflects potentially a real-life event, the timeline has shifted around to make it work in the narrative of the filmmaker. But again, the timeline and the narrative and all of it is fiction. And so, the motives and everything that is detailed in the film, none of that actually happened the way it’s depicted. For them to do that, what’s the motive of making that film? A lot is being made of that right now. What does that say about Hollywood? If you’re gonna make a fictional film, why do you use my name?
The reason you use it is because I’ve spent 45 years creating a very valuable brand, and they wanted to exploit it. They know that if they use the name “Chris Hansen,” people will come to the movie. Most of them will understand the movie is fiction, and there’s a graphic at the end of the film saying so. But that’s not the way it’s portrayed in the beginning of the film. And because there was such an attempt to imitate — although I think it was way more dramatic and over the top — my mannerisms and my lines and things I’ve said over the years, they turned it into a science fiction film, almost, with the greens and the vampire look of the character. It’s just over the top. In fact, it was so over the top, I was left wondering, “What’s the point of this?” And again, I’m not objective, because they exploited me and my brand and my name image for commercial enterprise. articles.title_orig: U.S. Bond Yields Hit Highest Level Since 2002
articles.title_zh: U.S. Bond Yields Hit Highest Level Since 2002
articles.content_orig:
The bond market is in an unrelenting sell-off. In the latest dubious milestone for US Treasuries, the yield on the 10-year benchmark note just hit its highest level since the dot-com bust.
American government bonds remain the world’s most important financial market, widely considered the safest place for investors to park their money. When times are tough, traders flee to the security of the US bond market.
That’s not what’s happening here. Just the opposite.
The reasons for the bond bust are numerous and, in some ways, counterintuitive: The US economy is strong – probably too strong, supported by massive AI spending . Inflation is too high, with prices pushed up by rising fuel costs. The Federal Reserve will probably try to slow all that down again.
The weak bond market and rising yields are hurting Americans’ borrowing power. Interest rates tied to the bond market, including mortgages and auto loans, continue to surge. The rate on a 30-year home loan topped 7% for the first time since early 2025 last week.
Meanwhile, investors keep heading for the bond market exits, selling off bonds and demanding higher rates at government bond auctions as inflation continues to rise. Higher prices degrade investments over time, and bondholders want to ensure they’re compensated for the effects of higher gas and diesel prices on their investments.
That’s sending yields ever higher, breaking through barriers not seen in decades. The 10-year yield on Thursday hit 5.34%, its highest level since 2002. The 30-year Treasury yield also hit a 24-year high, rising as high as 5.69%.
“There is carnage in the bond market,” said Neil Wilson, strategist at investment bank Saxo. “The worry is that US growth is way stronger than expected.”
Treasury yields pulled back on Thursday: The 10-year yield ended the day at 5.24%, still its highest level since 2007.
Analysts expect yields to remain elevated. US government data keeps showing evidence of a hot economy, maybe even an overheating economy.
A stronger-than-expected report on gross domestic product , the broadest measure of US economic activity, was released Wednesday, in addition to an inflation report that showed prices rising well above the Fed’s target. Some bondholders are sending yields higher in anticipation that the Fed will continue to raise its benchmark lending rate after increasing it last month for the first time since 2023 .
Why you should care about the bond market
Unemployment is low – the September jobs report on Friday is expected to show the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%, a level economists call “full employment.” Consumer spending remains robust, fueled by a strong stock market. And annual AI infrastructure spending is now measured in the trillions of dollars and is expected to keep growing – even as rates keep rising – over the course of the decade and beyond.
Debt concerns have also weighed on the bond market, as massive government spending from both political parties is putting the country on an unsustainable fiscal path.
The bond market’s problems are hardly isolated to the United States. Debt concerns and resurgent inflation as a result of high oil and fuel prices have sent rates higher all around the world. The 30-year UK government bond just hit 6% Thursday for the first time since 1998. The 10-year yield in France rose as high as 4.95% and hit its highest level since 2002.

articles.title_orig: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.title_zh: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.content_orig:
The family of Renee Good, from left; father Tim Ganger, mother Donna Ganger, brother Luke Ganger and brother Brent Ganger, listen during a news conference after the family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
The family of Renee Good , the 37-year-old killed last January by a federal agent during the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government Thursday.
One of the lawsuits, against the United States government itself, is essentially a wrongful death case, arguing that Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Good, violated his agency's own policies and the Fourth Amendment by using excessive force.
It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life. And also for her partner, Becca Good, who witnessed the killing. The lawsuit says she has suffered intense emotional distress from what she has experienced. Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car. At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.
The other lawsuit is rarer, alleging that federal officials engaged in a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of people in Minnesota.
It argues that Good's death was the "predictable and intended product" of the immigration crackdown in the state and that Ross' actions were in furtherance of a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic people the "object of aggression and abduction" and to silence the people "who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign."
In making that argument, the lawyers, with the firm Romanucci & Blandin, relied on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which was used to combat the terrorism wrought by the KKK during the Reconstruction era.
"I would say the second lawsuit is very unusual," Rachel Moran, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas, told NPR. "It was immediately striking to me because the Trump administration has been aggressively using conspiracy charges , including here in Minnesota, against people involved in protesting the administration's immigration tactics."
Moran said the lawyers in the Good lawsuits seem to be "turning that tactic on its head" by arguing that administration officials are involved in an illegal conspiracy themselves.
According to Ben Berkman, one of the lawyers representing Good's family, the first lawsuit is about what federal officers did to Renee Good on a Minneapolis street last winter. The second is about why those officers were on that street in the first place.
"It reaches the agent who fired those shots at Renee and it reaches every official who put him on the street that day," Berkman said. "No mask, no badge and no title in the administration puts anyone above that law."
Those federal officials include Ross, but also White House adviser Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House Border czar Tom Homan, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, among others. NPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but did not hear back.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We intend to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."
The lawsuit also lists 10 federal agents who were also present at the scene as John Does, noting that the federal government has not released their identities and that they were wearing masks at the time of the killing.
The civil charges also underscore a lack of criminal charges . DHS has provided little public indication that it is investigating Good's death or the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of Border Patrol agents a few weeks later in Minneapolis. According to The Trace, a news site that focuses on gun violence, nine people have been killed by immigration agents since President Trump took office again last year.
A memorial for Renee Good, who was killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January, remains in place at the site of her death, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
At the state level in Minnesota, local officials have also not filed charges or released the findings of any investigation. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, told NPR that state and local officials are reviewing the evidence and that they will "communicate transparently when a decision is reached."
At the press conference held Thursday, Good's family seemed frustrated at the inaction on all levels. Civil suits, like the ones filed by the family today, have the potential to hold entire institutions accountable rather than just individual actors.
"The fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Brent Ganger, Good's brother, said. "We will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability, for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."
Brent and his mother, Donna Ganger, also testified before Congress last week at a hearing about fatal shootings by federal immigration officers.
In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke. She focused her words on who Renee was to her, calling her kind and loving, but also on what she has lost. Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.
"This past August, I got ready to put our son in first grade. I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case, the whole nine yards. I went to Back To School Night on my own," Becca Good said. "She never missed a single moment. And this Halloween, it's our son's absolute favorite holiday. I'll take him trick or treating, without her hand in mine."
