Investigators have located the wreckage of a medical transport helicopter that crashed in the Pacific Ocean after departing Wednesday night from Santa Catalina Island, killing a pilot and a nurse.
One person, a female patient being taken to the mainland, remains missing, and two people survived. Sources familiar with the investigation said the missing woman is a 45-year-old resident of Avalon who suffered a severe allergy attack.
At a press conference Thursday, Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert Luna said it’s unlikely that the patient survived the crash, and noted the wreckage was deep in the water, 200 feet below the surface. Divers from the department’s special enforcement bureau will work with other agencies and use technology to search the ocean floor.
“This is a tragedy for Catalina and for Los Angeles County,” said county Supervisor Janice Hahn. “The men and women on board dedicated their careers to responding to crisis and saving lives. They are heroes.”
The Los Angeles County Fire Department received a call at 7:53 p.m. Wednesday for a marine rescue to pull three people from the water, agency spokesperson Jonathan Torres said.
The department learned that  the three were aboard a helicopter bound for the mainland and that five people were involved, Torres said. The aircraft was a Eurocopter EC135 P2, the National Transportation Safety Board said. The helicopter was equipped as a medical transport and was owned by REACH Air Medical Services, the U.S. Coast Guard said.
Flight tracking data show the helicopter left Catalina’s Pebbly Beach heliport and got about 175 feet above sea level about eight seconds into its flight before rapidly descending.
“We have a helicopter down right off of Pebbly Beach,” emergency dispatchers said over the radio, according to an audio recording of the incident. “We need Baywatch Avalon by boat. We’ve got a helicopter with potentially three people on board. ... We have people screaming for help.”
Rescuers found four people in the water. Two of them were pronounced dead, and two were rescued, taken to mainland hospitals  and were stable, Torres said. The fifth person has not been found, Torres said, though the search continued through the night and into Thursday.
The Coast Guard sent an MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter and crew to the island and deployed a 45-foot response boat to assist with the incident.
Leahy said the helicopter and boat are searching for the missing person across several square miles, and are using computer software that predicts where the person might be based on environmental factors such as drift and currents.
The longer the search continues, the larger the search area will have to be, he said. The crash left a large debris field that ocean currents have been pushing back toward the island, he said, which has made it easier for the L.A. County Sheriff’s Department to recover some of it, Leahy said.
If the missing person isn’t found, the search will eventually turn into a recovery, at which point the Coast Guard will disengage because the agency does not do body recoveries. When that could happen is unclear and depends on various factors, including how quickly the Coast Guard’s boat and helicopter can cover the search area. As of Thursday morning, conditions were relatively calm and good for searching, Leahy said, though the currents were stronger than expected.
Whether someone can survive in the water is also hard to predict, Leahy said, and depends on several factors, including the water temperature and whether the person is wearing a flotation device or is clinging to debris.
Aviation attorney Mike Slack, who is based in Austin, Texas, said the missing person most probably went down with the aircraft because patients are strapped to their gurney during helicopter transports for safety. That is a “real danger” during medical transports over water, he said.
Although it is too early to say exactly what caused the crash, Slack said that, with five people on board, a medical transport helicopter could exceed its maximum weight if it had a full tank of fuel.
Slack said the   NTSB will have little difficulty recovering the helicopter and extracting flight data despite the aircraft being underwater. Many helicopters are equipped with video and audio recording devices that capture everything inside, as well as flight and engine data recorders.
REACH Air Medical Services said in a statement on social media that it is aware of the incident and is gathering information and coordinating with authorities.
“Our thoughts are with the families, loved ones and colleagues affected by this tragedy,” the company said in its statement. “We are focused on supporting our team and everyone impacted during this incredibly difficult time.”
Federal aircraft records show the helicopter was manufactured by Eurocopter Deutschland GmbH, a German company.
The NTSB will lead the investigation, Torres said.
An NTSB spokesperson said that the agency’s investigators  arrived at the scene about 11:30 a.m. Thursday to document the site and examine the helicopter once it is recovered and transported to a secure facility.
“It is very early in the investigation, and limited information is available at this time,” the spokesperson wrote.
Catalina Island has one small hospital. About 250 people are transported to the mainland by helicopter each year for medical treatment, the hospital’s chief executive previously said .
Three people are in critical condition after miraculously surviving the impact of an air ambulance helicopter crash on Highway 50 in Sacramento on Monday night.
NTSB data show that of 13 incidents involving EC135 helicopters since 2005, not including Wednesday’s, six have involved fatalities. The last occurred in March 2025 in Canton, Miss., and involved a medical transport helicopter called AirCare 3. Three people died.
Wednesday’s fatal air disaster was also not the first involving a REACH Air Medical Services helicopter. Last October, a nurse aboard another REACH Eurocopter was killed, and the pilot and flight paramedic suffered serious injuries.
According to an NTSB preliminary report, “about 26 seconds” after the helicopter left UC Davis Medical Center heliport in Sacramento, “the flight paramedic reported the power had gone out and made a Mayday call as the chopper autorotated and crashed onto U.S. Route 50.”
An NTSB examination of the crash site found that an outer portion of the main rotor blade had broken off and was found stuck in a detached garage of a nearby home. The helicopter reached about 500 feet before an 11-second descent. A final report on the crash is still pending.
In November 2015, firefighters were using a REACH Eurocopter for training to simulate patient loading and unloading at the Apple Valley airport when the pilot felt a shudder and immediately landed. An NTSB investigation found that a towel had been ingested from an unsecured storage container on the ground, resulting in substantial damage to the tail rotor blades.

WASHINGTON —The Pentagon is dispatching a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as President Trump is reportedly weighing whether to ramp up the war against Iran after the midterms.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt and its strike group departed San Diego on Sunday, carrying up to 9,000 to 10,000 service members as Trump mulls over his next steps with Iran, the Wall Street Journal reported . The strike group is reportedly slated to arrive in November.
It’s not immediately clear if the deployment is intended to relieve another aircraft carrier in the region or add to the force posture there.
Already, the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington are stationed in the region, the latter of which relieved the USS Abraham Lincoln in August after its record-setting long deployment and allegedly bleak conditions for its crew. The USS George Washington is typically deployed in the Pacific Ocean and is ported in Japan.
Due to harrowing reports of weary sailors attempting to jump overboard amid shortages of critical supplies thanks to Iranian strikes that disrupted supply lines in the region, particularly a key port in Bahrain, the Pentagon made plans for the USS Theodore Roosevelt to be ready for a long stay.
This included maximizing its stash of food, hygiene, retail, and other critical supplies before its deployment, something Navy leadership touted last month .
They also took steps to ensure sailors will have more reliable communication with their families back at home and better quality of life amenities aboard the aircraft carrier.
“That means new entertainment equipment on the mess decks, more durable fitness equipment, spare cardio machines ready for our placement, and even holiday materials purchased ahead of time,” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said in a video announcement last motth about the reforms made.
The Post contacted the Pentagon and US Central Command for comment.
Last week, Trump rejected Iran’s proposed seven-day cease-fire offer , calling it unacceptable. Iran indicated it would open up the Strait of Hormuz during that time, but top administration officials have contended that the US is already getting oil through the critical chokepoint.

The president also indicated that he may resume a bombing campaign against Iran after the midterm elections.
“Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world,” he told Time magazine . “With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”

articles.title_zh: 'I know she's a liar': Nathan Fielder reveals more details from Elizabeth Holmes doc
articles.content_orig:
New York film festival: No spoilers here – TV’s grand illusionist meets his match when he moves in with Theranos founder and her family
F or anyone remotely near the worlds of documentary, comedy or medical fraud, there has been one thing on the mind for weeks now: a single-minute clip of Nathan Fielder , the absurdist comedian whose boundary-pushing HBO series The Rehearsal cemented his status as docu-reality’s premier auteur, staring into the deep blue eyes of Elizabeth Holmes , the disgraced founder of the blood-testing startup Theranos. Unblinking, faces inches apart, the famously dry purveyor of harebrained business schemes and the convicted fraudster appeared locked in a battle of wills. “Are you being real right now?” Fielder asked her, in a classically meta bit – could Fielder really have spent years filming a secret documentary with one of Silicon Valley’s most notorious pariahs?
The prospect of TV’s grand illusionist versus emblematic girl-boss scammer seemed potentially too good to be true; buzz for You Can See Everything, Fielder’s furtive documentary co-directed with wunderkind du jour Lance Oppenheim (whose narrative feature debut, the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime , premiered last month) was such that access to the film’s New York film festival premiere on Wednesday became this fall’s hottest ticket .
Those who were there can confirm: the hype is deserved. You Can See Everything is, somehow, more shocking, twistier, thornier and revealing than billed – a stupefying and gloriously destabilizing hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject. You know from the minute Billy Evans, Holmes’s shifty husband-cum-business partner who entered the picture post-Theranos, claims that “the best way for people to see who she is … is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”, while lying with Holmes on a playroom floor, that you’re in for a wild ride. My mouth was agape for, conservatively, one half of the film’s unusually deserved three-hour run time.
Let me say now, if you’ve made it this far: I will not spoil major shifts – and if you are at all familiar with the Fielder canon, you know they’re coming – for a singular movie whose enjoyment depends, in part, on an element of surprise, both for viewers and for film-makers who genuinely seem to not know what they signed up for when they walked into the Holmes-Evans household rental in 2023. Arguably the less you know about anything that is to come, the better.
What I can tell you is that You Can See Everything is a masterpiece of who’s playing who, the fragility and absurdities of trust, seemingly begotten by chance. Back in 2023, convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy and awaiting the start of her 11-year sentence in prison, Holmes, along with Evans – who appears to be her match made in heaven, as neither ever blink and are maybe always lying – sought out a film crew to document their life with their two young children, in an attempt to protest her innocence and, perhaps, rebrand for Theranos 2.0. For some reason, they chose Oppenheim, a documentarian whose distinctive style – hyper-saturation, tight frames, creeping zooms – exposes the eerie in the mundane, and Fielder, whose precise style of spectrum-y, extreme cringe means that no question will be off the table. As Fielder points out on camera, in one of several exquisitely blunt confrontations, it is an odd choice to allow a comedian famous for his business scams to make a documentary that will supposedly clear your name of arguably the most famous fraud scandal of the 2010s.
The result is a three-hour documentary filmed like a thriller and scored like a drama that plays like an unraveling of certainty in real time. Oppenheim’s house style, shots tightly hugging then boring into a face with laser-like curiosity, perfectly suits the material; scenes that could be an unlikely tableau instead become a fascinating parade of inscrutable motivations, isolated actors bristling against the others. There is something extremely satisfying in watching Fielder’s sharp angles – arched eyebrows, needling questions, dispensation of social buffers – tangle with Holmes’s disposition (or performance? or genuine personality?) of guileless warmth, a strange and compelling chemistry building within a reality distortion field. If Fielder’s earlier work felt at times like it was punching down, trading on the naivety of regular people, well, he has finally met his match.
I am, admittedly, writing around a film that must be seen to be discussed, and will surely engender much chatter as to what, exactly, we just witnessed. But trust that things devolve in a very Fielderian spiral, into a dissection of the form unlike anything I have ever seen or, as things get going and participants’ either lose their filters or sharpen their game, anything I have ever hoped to see when it comes to the figure known as Elizabeth Holmes . Trust, too, that if there was a question you were hoping to ask Holmes or, moreover, her husband – did he really have no reservations when he met the disgraced founder at a party in 2017, at the height of her scandal? – it gets asked, and then some (I did not need to know about conjugal visits, or lack thereof, in the Texas prison where Holmes continues to reside).
Trust, ultimately, that you can see more than you ever imagined you’d see about Elizabeth Holmes and maybe get no closer to discerning the truth – and yet it will all be worth it.

articles.title_orig: A new California law bans child marriage. What's the global outlook on the practice?
articles.title_zh: A new California law bans child marriage. What's the global outlook on the practice?
articles.content_orig:
A demonstrator in Massachusetts wearing a bridal gown takes part in a protest urging legislators to end child marriage. David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe/via Getty Images hide caption
It's been a landmark year for activists seeking bans against child marriage in the U.S. On Sept. 30, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Bill AB 1267 , setting 18 as the minimum age for marriage in the state, with no exceptions.
The bill, sponsored by Unchained at Last and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls, was authored by Assemblymember Gail Pellerin. It repealed provisions that had allowed minors to marry with parental consent and judicial approval, a system that meant California had no statutory minimum marriage age. The law also removes the parallel exception that allowed minors to enter domestic partnerships.
Its passage marks the culmination of a nearly decade-long campaign by survivors and advocacy groups to outlaw marriage before 18 in the state. California is now the 18th state to prohibit child marriage without exception; such marriages remain legal under varying restrictions in 32 other states.
The signing also brought survivor voices to the forefront. Newsom signed the measure alongside advocate Courtney Stodden, who was 16 when her parents permitted her to marry 50-year-old actor Doug Hutchison and has since become an outspoken campaigner against child marriage.
"The heart of this effort has always been the survivors," Pellerin said after the bill was signed. "They told us what it means to be a child in a marriage you did not freely choose."
She pointed to the difficulties minors can face in seeking legal help, leaving home or escaping adults who may be enabling the marriage. "Because of them, California children are safer."
The issue of child marriage — when one partner is under age 18 — is a global concern. The United Nations calls it a "human rights violation," citing a litany of concerns for child brides: "early pregnancy and social isolation, interrupting her schooling, limiting her opportunities for career and vocational advancement and placing her at risk of domestic violence." Yet every year, the U.N. estimates that 12 million girls become child brides.
Child grooms, the U.N. further notes, may be forced into "an adult role for which they are unprepared," with pressure to drop out of school and support a family.
The U.N. has set the goal of ending child marriage by the year 2030.
Since 2021, countries as diverse as Sierra Leone, England, the Philippines and the Dominican Republic have been passing legislation to set the marriage age at 18, with no exceptions.
In the United States, the current push for a national law is controversial — some have criticized provisions in the proposed legislation, and others oppose it altogether.
And legislation is not necessarily the solution. In India, marriage under age 18 is illegal, yet the latest National Family Health Survey conducted in country found that one in five women ages 20 to 24 married before turning 18. UNICEF estimates that at least 1.5 million girls under the age of 18 are married in India each year.
Even as states like California create new laws regarding child marriage, the United States as a whole is debating the issue — and raising the possibility of a nationwide ban.
On July 16, U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin and Sens. Dick Durbin, Brian Schatz and Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Child Marriage Prevention Act, a federal bill aimed at combating child marriage.
This legislation would push states toward a nationwide minimum marriage age of 18. "In 34 states, including Wisconsin, child marriage is legal. Many of these marriages are between young girls and adult men. It's time we end this predatory practice," Moore said in a statement emailed to NPR. "I know that advocates have pushed for reform at the state level, which has led some states to change their laws. This federal legislation would help bolster and support those efforts, including helping states get the data to understand its prevalence in their jurisdictions and then take action to address it."
In announcing the bill, its four congressional cosponsors cited data showing that more than 314,000 minors were legally married in the United States between 2000 and 2021, including girls as young as 10. The figures, compiled by child-marriage advocacy groups from state marriage records, indicate that most of the underage girls were married to adult men.
Unchained At Last, a nonprofit worked to end forced and child marriage in the U.S., estimates that at least 66,415 of these marriages — about one in five — occurred when the bride was at an age when sexual relations would be considered a crime (the age varies from 14 to 18 depending on the state). In roughly 90% of that subset, according to the organization's founder, Fraidy Reiss, marital exemptions in state statutory-rape laws shielded the adult spouse from prosecution . Married minors may also face legal barriers to hiring an attorney, filing for divorce or obtaining protection from abuse.
The Tahirih Justice Center, an organization with a long history of advocating for survivors of forced and child marriage, has been a key partner in developing and supporting this legislation.
"The one thing we hear all the time from places — Cameroon, Guatemala, you name it — is: 'It makes my work harder when a politician can say to my face, the United States allows child marriage, so why should I do anything?' The best thing that we can do to help the global movement is to get our house in order," says Casey Carter Swegman, director of public policy at Tahirih.
Swegman says that a child's apparent consent does not necessarily mean that the decision to marry was made freely. "A 15-, 16- or 17-year-old who has been pressured and coached by family members may tell a judge that she consents because refusing could expose her to punishment or violence at home," she says. This is especially troubling, Swegman says, when pregnancy, potential evidence of sexual abuse, is treated as justification for allowing the marriage to proceed.
"A child is coming before your court pregnant by an adult person — that should be a red flag for statutory rape, not a green light for marriage," she says.
Although the proposed bill has won support from many child-marriage advocates, others have questioned whether its provisions go far enough and warn of possible unintended consequences that it has overlooked.
"If I could heart a provision of this bill, it would be [the proposal] to provide financial incentive to states that have banned child marriage — that I can get behind," says Reiss. "While I applaud Congress for introducing and considering legislation to combat child marriage at the federal level, I am appalled that two sections of the Child Marriage Prevention Act would make a mockery of the bill's title."
Section 6, she says, would provide federal grants to states to "study" child marriage instead of banning it. "If states are given money to examine something that's a human rights violation instead of banning it outright, it would be devastating," says Reiss, who says she was forced to marry at age 19.
Section 10 would allow some minors as young as 16, whether in the United States or abroad, to qualify for a U.S. spousal visa under certain circumstances. This would actually encourage a particularly heinous form of child marriage, says Reiss: the trafficking of minors to the U.S. under the guise of marriage, and it would discourage U.S. states from setting their marriage age at 18, no exceptions. "If the bill were amended to set the spousal visa age at 18, it would be a 'game-changer' by sending a clear message to states and halting legal trafficking," she says.

Two years after a woman alleged a gang rape at Cornell University, renewed attention to the case and the limited consequences faced by the alleged perpetrators has raised questions about what higher education owes students who experience sexual assault on campus as well as how consent and intoxication are understood under New York law.
A woman identified as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging that she was sexually assaulted, gang-raped, and pressured to take drugs and drink alcohol by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19, 2024. The lawsuit is filed against the fraternity, Doe’s sorority chapter, and Cornell University; it names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, and Scott Kretzschmar as defendants. Prosecutors said this week they were reopening a criminal investigation into the case after declining to press charges originally.
Separate attorneys for Kretzschmar and Lopes denied the allegations in statements to ABC , while Norris, via an attorney, denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use but acknowledged that he sent a message included in the complaint.
When sexual assault allegations of this kind occur on campus, they can be addressed in three distinct ways: through school disciplinary proceedings, criminal proceedings, and civil lawsuits.
Doe’s civil lawsuit alleges that Cornell failed to protect her. Her attorney has separately criticized authorities’ handling of the criminal investigation, although observers say what’s known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in state law could limit what prosecutors are able to charge.
Here’s what to know about how the case was handled—by Cornell and the criminal justice system—before, and what could happen next.
Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police in November 2024. According to her complaint, Cornell began its Title IX investigation on Jan. 14, 2025.
Title IX is a law dating back to 1972 that is meant to, among other things, ensure that a college investigates when there is sexual assault on campus. Central to this premise is that Title IX is meant to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.

Doe’s attorney has said that Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students. Cornell has confirmed that its disciplinary process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, but has not disclosed individual outcomes. The lawsuit alleges negligence, breach of contract, and violations of New York law.

But women’s rights advocates believe that the school might not have fulfilled its legal obligations in investigating the incident and taking appropriate actions toward those involved.
Title IX is a federal civil rights law meant to prohibit sex-based discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.
Since Title IX was introduced, courts have found that the law requires institutions to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
“The reason why Title IX addresses sexual harassment, including sexual assault, is because of the very real impact that has on students’ ability to access education,” Shiwali Patel, a Title IX expert with the National Women’s Law Center, tells TIME.
According to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), students who experience sexual assault are more likely to earn lower GPAs in school and are more likely to drop out of school altogether.

Cornell told People that it works with students seeking to take leave or withdraw and “regularly refunds payments if students are no longer enrolled.”

Patel says it remains unclear whether Cornell fully complied with its Title IX obligations because the supportive measures it provided Doe are not publicly known.

Does she need some time off, some leave? Does she need a housing shift if the fraternity house and her sorority house are close together? Does she need counseling? Did they provide a stay away order? What kind of support were they giving her to make sure she wouldn’t have to be retriggered and traumatized by running into them?”
Title IX also requires schools to investigate allegations through a reliable, impartial process—independently of criminal court systems, and using a lower burden of proof to determine if a student violated campus policy.
Cornell University publicly disclosed that it was investigating the allegation on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe went to the police, according to the lawsuit. The university sent an alert to students regarding a report of sexual assault and coercion into taking drugs at a fraternity house. The same day, Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity.

The Biden Administration had expanded Title IX regulations in April 2024—taking effect in August 2024—broadening the definition of sexual harassment and extending federal protections.

House Democrats say officials may have illegally misused public funds to pay for president’s ‘narcissistic ego trips’
The Trump administration is facing growing questions over whether it illegally used taxpayer money to air television ads promoting Donald Trump five weeks before the US midterm elections .
Two congressional Democrats , Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California, have asked federal watchdogs to investigate the ads.
Raskin, the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives, and Whitesides wrote to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC) on Wednesday, describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”.
The first ad was initially broadcast on 23 September. It shows dozens of images of Trump as a singer repeats “love me”, and the UFC president, Dana White, praises the president. A second ad, which aired days later, pairs footage of Trump with audio from a rally criticizing the “deep state”. Both end with fine print saying they were paid for by the US government.
“President Trump is obviously desperate for the American people to ‘love’ him, a problem that goes beyond your jurisdiction,” Raskin and Whitesides wrote in their letter. “But stealing taxpayer dollars to pay for Mr Trump’s narcissistic ego trips is plainly illegal.”
The lawmakers asked the GAO to identify the source and total amount of money used, and to issue a legal decision on whether the ads broke the law. They asked the OSC to investigate and determine who should be held accountable.
The lawmakers say the ads may violate four sets of laws , and cited a provision in this year’s spending act that bars funds for “publicity or propaganda”, along with the Anti-Deficiency Act, federal criminal statutes on misusing public money and the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act exempts the president but covers executive branch staff, and the lawmakers argue that employees must have helped produce the ads.
Raskin and Whitesides reject the White House’s description of the ads as public service announcements. They say nearly every claim in them is false, and that they are virtually identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ads. In one example, they say an ad credits Trump with reviving manufacturing, though the US has lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs in his second term, according to a February report from Congress’s joint economic committee.
They also challenge the White House’s argument that the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot, though at an August rally he urged supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot”.
A White House spokesperson has called the ads “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. Trump said on Wednesday that he would “gladly pay the money” if the ads were found to be improper.

Some Republicans have also raised concerns. The Senate majority leader, John Thune, and the senators Mike Rounds, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis have questioned the use of public money, while the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair, Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said the ads were appropriate.
The ads are not the first administration advertising spending to draw scrutiny.
Last year the Department of Homeland Security under Kristi Noem spent more than $200m on ads promoting her and Trump’s immigration policies. In March, Noem testified that Trump had approved the campaign (which the president denied to Reuters), and he then removed her from the secretary role, relegating her to special envoy of the “Shield of the Americas”.

articles.content_orig:
What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
A review into what happened has been ordered and executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee said.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was carried out alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17. Shipp remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law.
Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out."
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have yet to give their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike was non-fatal, although medical experts have given theories.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC Pike probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause her breath to stop or heart failure.
The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility, while one of her lawyers said on Wednesday that she was being given "life-saving measures" in hospital.
On Thursday, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment."
He added: "But we do know that that she is alive right now."
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who said on Thursday that Tennessee will halt executions for the rest of the year.
This could impact any additional attempt by the state to execute Pike in the near-term, if she does regain consciousness.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years before.
A notable Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to try a second electrocution of Willie Smith, a black teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old.
The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment and Smith was executed aged 18.
"If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case.
Pike's lawyers have already filed a motion to stay her execution.
Mills said that if he was her lawyer, he would be asking both the federal courts and Tennessee court to reconsider their views on a second attempt and would also approach Governor Lee, who has powers to issue stays of executions and exercise clemency.
Opponents of the death penalty have been quick to react.
Maya Foa, the head of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain â lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
Why the death penalty is on the rise in US
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
Some manufacturers have explicitly said they will no longer produce pentobarbital or will restrict their use in executions, according to Alexis Hoag-Fordjor, Co-Director of the Center for Criminal Justice at Brooklyn Law School.
In 2024, for instance, the manufacturer Absolute Standards said it would no longer make the drug. , external
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
But the department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
"It's unclear, the quality and the effectiveness of the drug" used in Pike's execution, Hoag-Fordjor told the BBC, given how difficult it has been for states like Tennessee to obtain pentobarbital.
"It shouldn't be a surprise something went wrong," he said.
The predicament Tennessee authorities found themselves in - having to call emergency medical services to save Pike after trying to kill her - suggested there was "no plan in place" for a scenario like Pike's, Hoag-Fordjor added.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.
In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.

articles.title_zh: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
articles.content_orig:
We don’t yet know how the 2026 midterm elections will shake out.
What we can say right now is that President Donald Trump’s handling of inflation is a historic liability — the likes of which we’ve rarely seen in modern American politics.
As many as 8 in 10 Americans now disapprove of Trump on that issue. That’s more than disapproved of presidents for wars gone wrong, botched crisis responses and even major scandals like Watergate.
A new AP-NORC poll on Thursday was the latest ugly data point for Trump. It showed Americans disapproved of him on cost-of-living issues by a stunning margin: 82% to 17%.
It’s rare to get even 70% of Americans to agree on anything political. But Trump has managed to unite 8 in 10 Americans against his handling of one of the country’s most important issues.
And this poll isn’t just some outlier. Here’s a brief recap of recent polls on this issue:
The level of disapproval on such a major issue has few precedents, though George W. Bush did face a 77% disapproval rating in a CBS News/New York Times poll for his handling of the economy near the end of his term after the 2008 financial crisis. In 1980, the same pollster showed Jimmy Carter’s disapproval on that issue peaking at 74% amid high unemployment and inflation.
One of the likeliest culprits for such high disapproval numbers would seem to be war. And those have been very unpopular. But not as unpopular as Trump’s handling of the cost of living. George W. Bush’s disapproval rating on the Iraq war peaked around 70% . Disapproval of Joe Biden’s withdrawal from Afghanistan peaked around two-thirds . And the Vietnam war led Lyndon Johnson to scrap his reelection bid in 1968, but his disapproval rating on the issue was only in the 60s .
In fact, the highest disapproval rating for a war appears to be Trump’s latest numbers on the Iran war. The CNN poll showed 73% disapproved of his handling of that.
When it comes to crises, as many as 64% disapproved of Bush’s handling of Hurricane Katrina, and Carter’s disapproval amid the Iran hostage crisis climbed into the mid-50s. Even Trump’s handling of the January 6 attack on the Capitol ( 67% in CNN polling ) wasn’t as lopsided as Trump and inflation right now.
As far as scandals, Ronald Reagan’s disapproval on the Iran-Contra affair reached as high as 69% in a January 1987 Washington Post-ABC News poll. And at the height of Watergate, as many as 71% of Americans disapproved of Richard Nixon on domestic issues. (We don’t have good approval polling from back then on Watergate, specifically.)
Speaking of Nixon, pardons have also tested Americans’ tolerance. But even Gerald Ford’s pardon of Nixon — which was supposed to have crippled Ford politically — only saw a disapproval rating in the 50s , according to polls compiled by the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research.
Indeed, about the closest Trump got previously to 80% disapproval on a major issue was another controversial set of pardons: his pardons of violent January 6 defendants last year. A Pew Research Center poll showed 74% of Americans disapproved of that.
You might be noticing a trend here. Many of the issues with the highest presidential disapproval ratings involve the same president: Trump. That includes the Iran war, the January 6 Capitol attack and the related pardons. But the disapproval he faces on inflation surpasses all of those issues.
You could perhaps understand why Republicans are suddenly anxious to pass legislation on affordability before the election.
Trump in a new Time magazine interview published Thursday said Americans shouldn’t hold him responsible for their affordability problems and again blamed inflation on Biden. (This despite inflation being higher today than it was when Trump took over last year.)
But the AP-NORC poll is the latest to suggest that strategy won’t work. It shows 65% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for high prices more so than factors beyond his control. That number for Biden just before the 2022 midterm elections was much lower: 44% .
Perhaps Trump’s party can still do OK in the upcoming midterms. But if it does, it will be despite historic dissatisfaction with the president on voters’ clear No. 1 issue.

Business live – latest updates
The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.
In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.
Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.
“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”
Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war , as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.
The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.
The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

articles.title_zh: Disney’s Dana Walden on Jimmy Kimmel’s Late Night Future: “It’s Challenging”
articles.content_orig:
Television Business Editor
Dana Walden joked at the beginning of her Bloomberg Screentime session Thursday that her job was to “keep this seat warm for Casey Bloys, who’s bringing the real news.”
Disney’s president and chief creative officer stuck to that promise when asked about the future of Jimmy Kimmel Live! Kimmel signed a one-year contract extension in December 2025 to keep hosting the late night show through the 2026-27 season, and Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw asked Walden if the host would be sticking around.
“I’m not going to make that announcement here with you today,” Walden said. “Again, I’m letting Casey make the news.” (Bloys, the head of HBO and HBO Max, is the presumptive front-runner to head up streaming at the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery when that megamerger closes in the coming days.)
Speculation about Jimmy Kimmel Live! ‘s future has swirled since an early September Page Six story claimed Kimmel’s contract wouldn’t be renewed. ABC quickly denied that was the case, but other reports said the network is looking for significant budget cuts to keep the show going.
“The truth is, it’s a very challenging daypart,” Walden said Thursday at the Bloomberg event. “That’s not to say that Jimmy is not doing a phenomenal job, and his ratings are up. But they’re up relative to a smaller audience that’s watching late night on broadcast television.”
Kimmel and the show also have a big presence on YouTube and social media platforms, but those views and clicks bring in a fraction of the revenue that on-air advertising does. “That is not a lucrative opportunity for a very premium talk show,” said Walden.
“We’re trying to make sense of the business while also honoring a deep partnership,” she continued. “I love Jimmy; we have great friendship. He’s close to a number of the people at Disney. We’re trying to work through it and make sense of, what does Jimmy want, what’s the right thing to do, and what’s the right thing for our business.”

Sean Combs was reportedly placed back in solitary confinement following a NBC News report that the music mogul was using a contraband cellphone to scroll on Instagram, kept a private stash of premium liquor, and had access to a jailbroken tablet where he watched a Netflix documentary about himself.
The 56-year-old was put in a special housing unit, both NBC and TMZ have reported, after footage was released of Combs seemingly using a cell phone while serving his 50-month sentence at Fort Dix in New Jersey. This would be Combs’ second time placed in isolation, following a physical fight with a fellow inmate in July .
Last year, Combs was convicted on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution following a high-profile criminal trial. Combs recently had his release date bumped up to January 2028, though it is unclear if the apparent violation will push back his homecoming.
In a statement, Combs’ spokesperson chalked up the reporting of Combs’ time behind bars as sensationalization of “ordinary prison life,” adding that “the only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
According to NBC News, Combs had been enjoying a relatively pampered stay at the low-security federal correctional facility. The one-time billionaire reportedly had been directing thousands of dollars to fellow inmates in exchange for favors, including cooking him gourmet meals, and scrubbing down showers and toilets before he uses them. “He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” one source told the outlet. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
But beyond basic “pampering,” Combs allegedly has managed to secure contraband. He reportedly has a stash of Hennessy liquor, buys Remeron pills, a mood-boosting antidepressant drug, possess a jail-breaked tablet that he used to watch Netflix’s 50 Cent-produced docuseries about him, and has a cell phone that he uses to scroll on Instagram and view nude photos from an ex-girlfriend. Editorial Director/Box Office Editor
Well, on the bright side of things, the autumn box office should continue at a great hum this weekend thanks to Amazon MGM Studios’ feature take on the Colleen Hoover thriller Verity , starring Dakota Johnson, Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett. The domestic outlook is $30 million-plus at 3,510 theaters, with the definite potential to overperform given how there’s walk-up business from Hoover-philes.
The Michael Showalter-directed thriller also has a shot at $20M-$25M in 70 offshore territories sans Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and CIS in this suite, which would be a $50M-$55M global start. Previews stateside start Thursday on Verity at 2 p.m.
Meanwhile, light candles and say prayers for Warner Bros/Legendary Entertainment’s Tom Cruise -starring, Alejandro G. Iñárritu-directed Digger . Many are bracing for what could be one of Cruise’s lowest wide openings at the box office of the millennium. Warners believes the movie can get to $12M-$15M at 3,300 theaters; others believe it’d lucky to break $10M at the domestic box office.
Seventy-three foreign territories except Poland, Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand (no China release) are expected to deliver another $15M-$20M abroad for Digger at 14,000+ screens, which would mean a $35M global start at the high end for the reported net $125M production (rumors suggest the movie cost much higher, between $140M-$150M).
Unlike the Dune franchise, Legendary didn’t co-finance Digger , but they did produce it. Previews start at 2 p.m. in North America, with tickets on sale in Imax, Dolby Cinema, VistaVision, PLFs and motion seats.
Digger was shot at Leavesden Studios with UK tax credits; the global marketing spend is approaching $100M. To say that the movie is divisive is an understatement, with some critics hailing the brilliance of the polemic movie and its Doctor Strangelove satire, while others were simply impatient watching it. Current Rotten Tomatoes critical score is 52%, and know that Cruise has had lower ratings (2017’s The Mummy was 15% Rotten with reviewers, and 2016’s Jack Reacher: Never Go Back was 37% Rotten). Warners in a last-minute marketing salvo is leaning into selling the controversy of the film with a final spot, this tweet having clocked 2.2 million views:
Decide for yourself. DIGGER – in theaters and IMAX FRIDAY. Tickets on sale now. https://t.co/Z1IpSpFnXd pic.twitter.com/e5ID4WUxbL
Back in his heyday as a star, Cruise posted low openings at the domestic box office in the single-digit range (i.e., the classic Rain Man opened to $7M in 1988 at 1,248 theaters and powered to $172.8M domestic), but those were different distribution days when movies opened small and played long. Post-2000, some of Cruise’s lowest North American opening have included the 2007 drama Lions for Lambs ($6.7M; $35M production cost), 2012’s Rock of Ages ($14.4M; $75M production cost), Jack Reacher ($15.2M and $60M production cost, though it spawned a Prime Video TV franchise) and 2017’s American Made ($16.7M; $60M net production).

However, on a seismic bomb level, 2017’s The Mummy at $31.6M domestic opening/$172.6M worldwide wasn’t enough to save that $195M production, which finaled at $80.2M domestic, $409.2M WW. The arguments made for his spendy Mission: Impossible movies, particularly the last two, is that they’re bound to profit in their nth cycle (You gotta look at the overall library not just the individual movie, Paramount says in defending that franchise).
What positive things are there to say about Digger at this point? Domestic tracking in first choice climbed from a 2 since landing on tracking to a 7, which is the same as Cruise’s American Made and higher than Marty Supreme ($17.7M opening). Who wants to see this movie? Best first choice right now is men over 25, which is above the tracking figures for American Made and Marty Supreme .

Back to Verity. We hear U.S./Canada presales are behind It Ends With Us ($50M opening; $148.5M domestic final, $351.4M WW) , but that’s not a bad thing. That movie was Hoover’s most popular novel, and it opened when Blake Lively was in the mega-ether of Deadpool & Wolverine. Not to mention female audiences were intrigued by the percolating crisis between Lively and her co-star/director Justin Baldoni (fans were already deconstructing bad blood between them from red-carpet photos alone).
Hollywood went on a buying spree, snapping up Hoover tomes for the big screen. Two of them, Paramount’s Regretting You ($13.6M opening, $48.8M domestic, $90.4M WW) and Reminders of Him ($17.9M opening, $48.5M domestic, $89.2M WW) were all right in regards to their budgets, but not box office sensations. Verity is arguably Hoover’s second-most popular novel.
Like-for-like comps for Verity abroad are above The Drama ($9.4M international opening), lit thriller Where the Crawdads Sing ($12M) and Reminders of Him ($10M, though that was in 56 territories). The lit adaptation should do well in Europe, specifically Scandinavia, and we’re hearing advance ticket sales are really hot in Brazil, where Verity is above It Ends With Us. In like-for-likes, It Ends With Us had a $45.6M opening.

Also opening stateside in 1,350 theaters this frame is Lionsgate Premiere’s horror pic Beware Boiuna from filmmaker Mike P. Nelson, which is looking at single digits. Blurb: A team of doctors embark on a local mission in the Amazon rainforest, but it soon becomes clear that not everybody — or everything — is happy to see them. Their sudden appearance draws the attention of an animal predator, the “Boiúna.”
Meanwhile, don’t count out A24’s Primetime. Many thought the pic would be front-loaded, but it has posted solid weekdays and is now up to a running total of $23.8M. The Lance Oppenheim-directed movie starring Robert Pattinson could hold to better than -60%.
Older adults will continue to go to Paramount’s Brad Pitt survival movie The Heart of the Beast, with a second-weekend dip of around 40%. Its U.S./Canada cume currently is $26M. Last weekend’s Avengers Endgame: Encore looks to decline around 60% in its second weekend. The reissue with extra Avengers: Doomsday footage stands at $31.1M.

Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
Business live – latest updates
The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.
In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.
Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.
“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”
Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war , as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.
The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.
The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out a ceasefire on long-range strikes with Ukraine as Moscow steps up its campaign of aerial attacks on Kyiv .
“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships.’ It is simply ridiculous,” Putin said on Thursday at the Valdai political forum in Moscow.
The remarks followed a meeting between United States President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on September 22, when Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow also stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Speaking at the forum of the Moscow-based think tank, Putin said Ukraine had “partially achieved its objectives” with ⁠these strikes, with attacks on Russian ⁠oil refineries having cost the country 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), but added that Russia ⁠was now responding in kind.
Russia has ramped up long-range strikes, targeting Ukraine’s steel companies as well as supply chains, notably in the rail sector. Ukraine accuses Moscow of deliberately hitting civilian targets and keeping Kyiv on a near-constant state of alert as it braces for another tough winter.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, according to city officials, as the Ukrainian capital endured relentless aerial attacks. No casualties were reported as children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit.
Putin added that Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted it to ⁠be a neutral ⁠country after the end ⁠of hostilities.
He warned the West not to escalate the standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania, and pledged to defend it with nuclear weapons if necessary.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well – the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda,” he said.
Putin’s comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia’s Baltic exclave.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict ⁠could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios. “We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” ⁠he said.
On the contrary, in the event of a “favourable scenario”, Putin said the assets of Western companies that Moscow had seized could potentially be returned. Putin last month ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro.

articles.title_zh: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.content_orig:
Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The disgraced hip-hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.
They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which include video of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.
“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.
TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.
Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.
“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.
Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.
“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.
Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or gray sweatpants and shirts.
Meals are delivered in trays, but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.
“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.
It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.
He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.
The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)
“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.
Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein .

articles.title_orig: China’s Fuel Export Halt: Is Beijing Turning Energy Security Into Geopolitical Leverage?
articles.title_zh: China’s Fuel Export Halt: Is Beijing Turning Energy Security Into Geopolitical Leverage?
articles.content_orig:
Beijing is not wielding diesel as a weapon. It is doing something with longer consequences: putting its own fuel security openly ahead of its role as Asia's swing supplier — and making every importer in the region bargain for what used to be a market.
A Holiday Notice That Moved the Oil Price
On Wednesday, on the eve of China’s Golden Week holiday, PetroChina cancelled most of the gasoline and jet fuel cargoes it had committed for October, many of them agreed only in the previous fortnight. By Thursday, according to four people briefed on the decision, Chinese refiners had suspended fuel exports to everywhere except Hong Kong and Macau until further notice. There was no public announcement; the news leaked through traders.
Markets reacted anyway. US crude turned an early loss into a rally to around $91.50 , and diesel in Asia traded about $75 a barrel above the crude it is made from. In a fuel market already short of millions of barrels a day, a quiet instruction to Chinese refiners proved as powerful as an OPEC meeting. The question is what Beijing intends to do with that power.
China has the world’s largest refining system, able to process roughly 18.8 million barrels a day . Its fuel exports have always been tightly managed through quotas, but in normal times they made China a reliable source of diesel, petrol and jet fuel for Asia. In 2024, by one estimate, China supplied a third of Australia’s jet fuel and about half of the fuel used by the Philippines and Bangladesh .

That role has been switched on and off all year. Beijing curbed exports in March as the Iran war closed Hormuz, then eased them in mid-July. In August China exported 6.01 million tonnes of oil products, up 12.7% on a year earlier. That surge drained its own tanks: by late September commercial gasoline stocks were at their lowest since 2011 and diesel stocks at their lowest since 2015.
The tempting reading is that Beijing is weaponising fuel, as Russia weaponised gas in 2022. The evidence does not support it. This halt is driven by domestic need, and part of that need was created in Washington.
Start with supply. Between a fifth and a quarter of China’s refining capacity sits in independent “teapot” refineries in Shandong province, whose business model depended on discounted Iranian crude. Since the United States reimposed its blockade of Iranian oil on 13 July, those barrels have dried up and the discount has turned into a premium. As Modern Diplomacy has reported, physical interdiction has achieved what a decade of sanctions could not: the teapots cannot sanction-proof this war . With independent refiners cutting runs and domestic demand recovering seasonally, China’s surplus of fuel to export has shrunk sharply.
Then look at the law. China’s Energy Law, in force since January 2025, made holding strategic reserves a legal obligation for state and private companies. China built crude stocks of roughly 1.1 to 1.2 billion barrels — about 100 days of import cover — before the war began. A state that thinks this way does not need a geopolitical motive to stop exporting fuel when its own tanks run low. Security comes first by statute.
But hoarding still creates leverage. Leverage does not require intent; it requires that others depend on your discretion. Here the record is instructive. When Beijing first banned exports in March, deepening Asia’s fuel shortage , it quietly kept diesel flowing to the Philippines and Vietnam, both rivals in the South China Sea. That undercuts the coercion story: a state bent on punishment would have starved Manila first. Yet it confirms the larger point. Supply was allocated by Beijing, cargo by cargo, rather than by price. As one analyst put it at the time: “China restricts supplies rather than coming to the rescue.” Neighbours have learned that Chinese fuel is available when China has spare product, and on China’s terms when it does not. That uncertainty is a form of power, even if no one in Beijing designed it as one.
The damage travels well beyond Asia, because fuel markets are connected by price, not by geography. China ships little diesel directly to Europe. But when Chinese barrels vanish from Asia, Asian buyers bid for Indian, Korean and Middle Eastern cargoes that would otherwise sail west. Europe was counting on the opposite: traders had expected Chinese refiners to add more than a million tonnes of diesel to international markets in September. Now the Indian refiners that have been filling Europe’s gap face a stronger pull from Asia. The halt also lands as Russia keeps its own diesel export ban in place until 31 October and Washington debates restrictions. Three of the world’s most flexible fuel exporters are putting their home markets first at the same time.
That is where inflation comes in. Diesel moves goods and powers farm machinery, so its price feeds directly into freight and food costs. US distillate stocks are already 14% below their five-year average. In Asia, which burns 38% of the world’s oil, the IMF had already raised its forecast for regional inflation to 2.6% this year , up from 1.4% in 2025, and named Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Cambodia among the most exposed. A prolonged Chinese halt would push that figure higher.
The strongest objection is that this is temporary: a holiday-period pause by refiners guarding stocks, which will ease once inventories rebuild, as it did in July. Exports will probably resume in some form. But the pattern of this year — curb, ease, curb again, each time without warning — is itself the change. Analysts at Energy Aspects expect Beijing to hold clean-fuel exports to around 1.2 million tonnes a month in the fourth quarter, less than half of July’s 2.55 million tonnes. Even a “resumption” would leave Asia far shorter than before.
Base case (around 55%) — exports return, but rationed. After Golden Week, Beijing issues a reduced quota in the region of 1.2 million tonnes a month. Asian diesel and jet margins stay near record levels, more Indian and Korean cargoes are pulled east, and Europe’s winter shortfall widens. No dramatic crisis follows, only a higher fuel bill everywhere. This rests on Gulf refineries continuing their slow recovery and no further loss of crude supply to the teapots.
Downside case (around 25%) — the halt runs through the winter. Inventories fail to recover because the teapots stay short of crude and winter demand rises. Russia extends its ban beyond October and Washington imposes even partial diesel export limits. With China, Russia and the US all restricting at once, the poorest Asian importers ration fuel — Bangladesh and Sri Lanka first — and regional inflation overshoots the IMF’s forecast. In this scenario, Beijing’s allocation of whatever it does export becomes openly diplomatic: who gets cargoes, and on what terms, becomes a question for foreign ministries rather than traders.
Upside case (around 20%) — a deal refills the teapots. A US-Iran settlement lifts the blockade, Iranian crude flows back to Shandong, and Gulf refineries recover faster than expected. Beijing issues a generous quota and presents it as a contribution to regional stability. Prices ease, but the lesson remains: relief arrived because China chose to give it.
China is not yet using fuel as a weapon. It has done something that may matter more in the long run: it has made clear, through law, stockpiles and repeated export halts, that its fuel security outranks its role as the region’s supplier. In a market this tight, that ranking is itself leverage. Asia, and indirectly Europe, now buys Chinese fuel at Beijing’s discretion rather than at a market price.
